lesson.menu_desc: Three people who changed schools, and the words that say HOW BIG a difference is -- far, considerably, slightly, and the more ... the more -- 26 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- Two Schools
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Sophia | Lesson 6 -- Two Schools
lesson.grammar_point: comparative modifiers (far / considerably / slightly) and the more ... the more

listenings.text: Everyone asked me the same question after I changed schools, and it was always the wrong question: is the new one harder? It is not harder. It is differently hard. The math is a good deal easier, the history is far more reading than I have ever done, and English went from four hours a week to fifty minutes, which nobody thinks is a problem until you notice your own accent getting worse. In the first term I was slightly behind in two subjects and a long way ahead in one, and I spent the whole time worrying about the wrong one. So this is what I would say to anybody who is moving. The more you hold on to the subject you were already good at, the less you lose. Nobody takes it away from you. You put it down yourself.

Good morning, and welcome to the recorded introduction for families joining us this term. A few practical points before your visit. The school day here begins at seven fifty and ends at one thirty, which for most of you will be slightly earlier than you are used to. The timetable is issued in the first week and it does not change after that, so keep it somewhere safe. Our written workload is considerably heavier in the first term than in the second. That is deliberate, and students who fall behind early tend to stay behind, so please speak to your grade coordinator in the first two weeks rather than the second. Assignments are set on Monday and collected on Friday. And one request from us: the more you tell us in September, the less we have to guess in March.

paras: MAYA, 13. I changed schools in the middle of the year, from one where half the day was in English to one where English is a single class a week. The new building is far bigger, and my timetable is only slightly longer, so on paper almost nothing changed. In practice everything did. The workload here is considerably heavier, and for the first month I was certain I would fall behind in every subject except English. What actually happened was stranger: I am a good deal better than the others at English and a good deal worse at Italian, and the more I try to keep up in one, the more I forget about the other. Nobody warned me that changing schools is mostly a problem of time, not of brains.

DANIEL, 12. Everybody told me the new place would be much stricter. It is not, particularly -- the rules are marginally tighter and that is all. What is genuinely different is the teachers. At my old school they explained a rule and then we used it for twenty minutes; here they explain for forty and we use it for five. My English is slightly worse than it was a year ago, which I did not expect, and my written Portuguese is far stronger. The assignments are longer but easier. I got used to the place faster than my sister did, and she is two years older than me. The more I sit and listen, though, the less I remember -- that part has not changed, and I do not think it is going to.

PRIYA, 13. My old school was considerably smaller: one class per year, and everybody knew everybody. This one has nine hundred students, and I was sure that would be the hard part. It was not. The hard part was that the level in English here is far lower than what I was used to, so for a whole term I stopped working at it and my speaking got noticeably worse while my grades got better. That is the trap, and nobody sees it coming. Now I do thirty minutes of my own every evening -- a series, a podcast, anything -- and the more I do outside school, the less it matters what happens inside it. A demanding school is a gift. A comfortable one you have to work around by yourself.

gist.prompt: What do the three of them agree about?
choices: All three of them say the new school is far worse than the old one.
In each one, the thing everybody had warned them about was not the real difference.
None of them managed to keep up after changing schools.

items: Maya's school day is much longer than it used to be.
“my timetable is only slightly longer” -- the change is real, and it is small. That one word is the whole difference.
Daniel spends more time listening to explanations than he used to.
“they explained a rule and then we used it for twenty minutes; here they explain for forty and we use it for five.”
Priya's English improved as soon as her grades did.
The opposite: “my speaking got noticeably worse while my grades got better.” That is what she calls the trap.
Daniel needed less time than his sister to settle into the new school.
“I got used to the place faster than my sister did, and she is two years older than me.”

items.situation: Somebody asks whether your school is harder than your last one. Do not answer with harder or easier -- say how much.
tips: It's considerably harder in Italian and only slightly harder in English.
It's far more work, but the classes are a bit shorter.

items.situation: Compare two teachers you have had, without saying that either of them is bad.
tips: She explains a good deal more slowly, which suits me better.
He gives marginally more homework, but he checks all of it.

items.situation: Your friend says: the more homework they give, the less anybody learns. Agree with her, and add your own version.
tips: True -- and the more subjects you have, the harder it is to keep up with any of them.
The more I do during the week, the less I have to do at the weekend.

items.situation: Name one thing about your week that has changed only slightly, and one that has changed enormously.
tips: My timetable is slightly longer. My Italian is far better than it was.
The way to school is a bit shorter; the workload is considerably bigger.

items.situation: You do not know the English word for something at school. Describe it instead of switching to Portuguese.
tips: It's the paper that tells you which class you have and when.
It's the person who takes the class when your teacher is away.
